summary: Show a polycrystal as differently oriented lattice domains and make slip planes a property of orientation rather than a texture.
objective: Build a polycrystalline block where each grain has its own lattice orientation and I can reveal the slip planes that follow it.
intent_signals: Show why a metal has grains with different orientations.
Explain slip planes and grain boundaries in a 3D block.
example_prompts: Build a polycrystalline block with per-grain lattice orientation and toggleable slip planes.
Show a dislocation stepping through a lattice plane and where a grain boundary interrupts it.

entities.name: Grain domains
entities.guidance: Partition the block into grains as closed cells with shared boundary faces, each storing its own lattice orientation.

entities.name: Lattice and slip planes
entities.guidance: Draw a sparse lattice inside a selected grain and derive the highlighted plane from that grain orientation, so the plane rotates with the grain.

entities.name: Dislocation marker
entities.guidance: Show one dislocation line and its step-by-step advance along a plane, stopping visibly at the grain boundary.

state_contract.model: Grain list with orientations, a boundary set shared between neighbouring grains, and a dislocation position expressed as a step index on a chosen plane. Each grain declares a lattice type whose slip plane and slip direction families come from defaults.values.state_table, so the planes drawn in a grain are generated from its lattice and orientation rather than authored per grain. Deformation shown is an authored illustration, not a computed response to load.
state_contract.authority: Grain orientation is authoritative: lattice, slip plane and dislocation direction are all derived from it, so changing an orientation must update all three together.
actions: Select a grain and show its lattice and available slip planes.
Step a dislocation along the selected plane.
Toggle the grain boundary surfaces and the outer block faces.
Reset orientations and the dislocation to the authored start.

invariants: A slip plane never crosses a grain boundary unchanged; at the boundary the plane orientation changes or the marker stops.
Neighbouring grains share one boundary surface rather than each owning a private copy.
Stepping the dislocation backwards restores the previous lattice state exactly.
motion_guidance: Advance the dislocation in discrete lattice steps so the motion reads as bond-by-bond, not as a sliding decal.
Do not deform the whole block continuously as if a load were applied; any shape change is an authored illustration.
known_limits: Illustrative microstructure: grain sizes, shapes and orientation distribution are authored, not from a measured sample.

The cited slip-system page gives system counts for cubic close-packed (12, five independent) and hexagonal close-packed (3, two independent) but names only the plane and direction family for body-centred cubic, so no b.c.c. count is claimed here.
The recipe shows one dislocation on one plane; multiplication, tangles and cross-slip are out of scope.
Schmid's law here selects a primary system geometrically; it is not a plasticity solver and predicts no stress-strain curve.
Authored guidance only: no scene runtime, rendering or numerical calibration has been run for this recipe.

claims.statement: A slip system is the combination of a slip plane and a slip direction. Cubic close-packed metals slip on <1-10>{111}, with three distinct directions in each of the four {111} planes making 12 distinct slip systems, five of which are independent. Hexagonal close-packed metals slip on <100>{001}: there is only one distinct {001} plane and three distinct <100> directions in it, giving three distinct slip systems and only two independent ones. Body-centred cubic metals slip on <1-11>{110} and have no close-packed planes; the cited page names that family without giving a system count. The von Mises criterion quoted there requires a minimum of five independent slip systems for general yielding.
claims.scope: Slip plane and direction families, distinct and independent system counts where the page states them, and the five-independent-system yielding criterion. No body-centred cubic count is claimed, and no temperature or strain-rate dependence is covered.

source_refs.locator: Introduction: "The combination of slip plane and slip direction together makes up a slip system". Slip in CCP metals: "There are 3 distinct slip directions lying in this plane, and there are 3 other planes of the {111} type, making 12 distinct slip systems of the <1 bar1 0>{111} type"; "There are 12 such <1 bar1 0>{111} systems, five of which are independent". Slip in HCP metals 1: "there is only one distinct lattice plane of the {001} type"; "the h.c.p. structure exhibits three distinct slip systems"; "The h.c.p structure has only two independent slip systems". Which slip system will operate?: methods work "only for cubic crystals that slip on <1 bar1 0> {111} or <1 bar1 1> {110}, i.e. cubic close-packed (c.c.p) or body-centred cubic (b.c.c.) metals respectively". Summary/Questions: "the von Mises criterion states that a minimum of five independent slip systems must exist for general yielding"; "Body-centred cubic metals are also ductile through the mechanism of slip, but they have no close-packed planes"

claims.statement: The resolved shear stress on a slip system under a tensile stress is tau_R = (F/A) cos(phi) cos(lambda), where phi is the angle between the tensile axis and the slip plane normal and lambda the angle between the tensile axis and the slip direction; slip begins when tau_R reaches the critical resolved shear stress, so Schmid's law reads tau_C = sigma_y cos(phi) cos(lambda) and the primary slip system is the one with the greatest Schmid factor cos(phi) cos(lambda). In the cited cadmium example (a = b = 2.98 A, c = 5.62 A, tensile axis [021], slip on the [010](001) system) phi_0 = arctan(2a/c) = 46.7 degrees, lambda_0 = 43.3 degrees, the Schmid factor is 0.499, and with a critical resolved shear stress of 0.15 MPa and a 3 mm crystal diameter the force required to cause slip is 2.12 N.
claims.scope: Geometric selection of the primary slip system and one worked single-crystal force calculation. It does not predict polycrystal yield strength, work hardening or rate dependence.

source_refs.locator: Slip geometry: the critical resolved shear stress - "tau_R = F cos lambda / (A / cos phi) = (F/A) cos phi cos lambda"; "This is Schmid's Law. The quantity cos phi cos lambda is called the Schmid factor"; "tau_C = sigma_y cos phi cos lambda"; "the primary slip system will be the system with the greatest Schmid factor". Slip in HCP metals 2 and 3: "Cadmium is (approximately) hexagonal close-packed with a = b = 2.98 A and c = 5.62 A, and it slips on <100>{001}", tensile axis [021]; "phi_0 = tan^-1(2a/c) = tan^-1(2 x 2.98 / 5.62) = 46.7 deg", "lambda_0 = 90 deg - phi_0 = 43.3 deg", "cos 46.7 x cos 43.3 = 0.499", "F = tau_c A / (cos phi_0 cos lambda_0) = 0.15 x 10^6 x pi x (1.5 x 10^-3)^2 / 0.499 = 2.12 N"

defaults.rationale: The slip-system table, the counts and the Schmid-law numbers all restate the cited DoITPoMS package (claim.polycrystal-slip-system-families, claim.polycrystal-schmid-law); dislocation motion as the carrier of plastic deformation restates claim.rd-dislocation-slip. The body-centred cubic row deliberately carries no system count: the page names the <1-11>{110} family and says b.c.c. metals have no close-packed planes, but never prints a count, so inventing 12 or 48 here would be fabrication. Grain count, grain size and the number of dislocation steps stay authored scene choices because the source is about single-crystal geometry, and they are marked as such. Tunable: change grain count and orientations freely, but the plane and direction families per lattice are not tunable, they are the sourced content.

worked_example.inputs: Two questions on the same scene: (a) count the c.c.p. and h.c.p. slip systems from plane and direction multiplicities; (b) a cadmium h.c.p. single crystal, a = 2.98 A, c = 5.62 A, tensile axis [021], slip system [010](001), critical resolved shear stress 0.15 MPa, crystal diameter 3 mm
worked_example.expected: (a) c.c.p. 4 x 3 = 12 distinct systems, 5 independent; h.c.p. 1 x 3 = 3 distinct systems, 2 independent, so an h.c.p. grain fails the von Mises minimum of 5 while a c.c.p. grain exactly meets it. (b) phi_0 = 46.7 deg, lambda_0 = 43.3 deg, Schmid factor 0.499, force at slip 2.12 N
worked_example.derivation: (a) The {111} family has 4 distinct planes and each contains 3 distinct <1-10> directions: 4 x 3 = 12, of which the source states 5 are independent. The {001} family has 1 distinct plane containing 3 distinct <100> directions: 1 x 3 = 3, of which 2 are independent. Compare each against the sourced von Mises minimum of five independent systems. (b) phi_0 = arctan(2a/c) = arctan(2 x 2.98 / 5.62) = arctan(1.0605) = 46.7 deg; because tensile axis, slip direction and plane normal are coplanar here, lambda_0 = 90 - 46.7 = 43.3 deg; Schmid factor = cos 46.7 x cos 43.3 = 0.686 x 0.728 = 0.499; A = pi (1.5e-3)^2 = 7.07e-6 m^2; F = tau_c A / 0.499 = 0.15e6 x 7.07e-6 / 0.499 = 1.06 / 0.499 = 2.12 N.

tolerance.counts: exact integers; a grain whose generated plane set does not match its lattice row is a defect, not a rounding difference
tolerance.angles_deg: +/- 0.1 deg against the sourced 46.7 and 43.3 values
